questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace an identity comparison between two bindings of the same small integer
questions.stem:
Two names are bound to the same small integer literal in separate statements. What does this program print?

a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b, a == b)

options.text: True True
False True
options.misconception: believes every literal allocates a fresh object so identity is always false

options.text: True False
options.misconception: believes a shared object means the two names cannot also compare equal

options.text: False False
options.misconception: believes both operators fail once an integer is large enough to need two digits

questions.explanation: The interpreter keeps one shared object for every small integer, so both names reach that one object and the identity test succeeds. The tempting answer assumes each literal is a separate allocation, which is what happens for values outside that small range and not for the short ones written out in full. Equality succeeds either way, because the two names hold the same value no matter how many objects happen to back it.
questions.hint: Ask whether writing the same short literal twice really allocates twice.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: select the operator that asks whether two names refer to one object
questions.stem: A program must establish whether two variable names are attached to one shared object, not merely whether the values read the same. Which operator performs that test?

options.text: is, which asks whether both names reach one shared object
==, which asks whether both names reach one shared object
options.misconception: believes the equality operator compares object addresses rather than values

options.text: ==, which asks whether both values carry exactly the same type
options.misconception: believes the equality operator is really a type check on the two operands

options.text: is, which asks whether both values carry exactly the same type
options.misconception: believes the identity operator additionally verifies that types match

questions.explanation: The identity operator compares whether two references land on the very same object without inspecting the contents. The equality operator asks whether the values are indistinguishable, which two separately built lists of matching contents can be while occupying different storage. The tempting pairing swaps the two, and that swap causes most identity bugs: asking for identity with equality reports a shared object as distinct, and asking for equality with identity reports two equal values as different.
questions.hint: One operator compares storage, the other compares what is stored. Decide which the question needs.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace an equality and identity comparison on a string assembled at run time
questions.stem:
The second name is filled in at run time rather than written as a literal. What does this program print?

a = "hello"
b = "".join(["he", "llo"])
print(a == b, a is b)

options.text: True False
True True
options.misconception: believes matching character data forces the interpreter to reuse one object

options.text: False False
options.misconception: believes a run-time join cannot reproduce the characters of a literal

options.text: False True
options.misconception: believes the literal is the derived value and the join yields the original

questions.explanation: Joining builds a fresh string object at run time, so the two names hold equal contents in different storage. Equality compares contents and therefore succeeds, while identity fails because nothing is shared. The tempting answer assumes the interpreter searches for an existing object whenever a string is produced, which would make identity testing useless for exactly the run-time values a program most needs to tell apart.
questions.hint: Trace where each name's storage came from, then ask whether the two names share it.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace a mutation made through a second name bound to the same list
questions.stem:
The second name is bound from the first, and the growth happens through the second. What does this program print?

first = [1, 2]
second = first
second.append(3)
print(first, second)

options.misconception: believes binding a second name snapshots the list at that moment
believes the growth lands on a copy made when the name was bound
believes growth affects only the name it is called on and no other

questions.explanation: A list is a mutable object, and binding a second name to it attaches that name to the same object rather than to a copy of its contents, so any change made through either name shows through the other. The tempting answer imagines a snapshot taken at binding time, but a plain assignment never inspects or duplicates the object, which is also why a function handed a list can change the caller's list without being asked to.
questions.hint: Ask whether the assignment duplicated the object or only attached another name to it.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: identify the single truthy value among four commonly confused literals
questions.stem: Four values are tested in plain conditions. Which one of them is the only truthy value?

options.text: the non-empty string holding the character zero
the integer zero itself as a bare value
options.misconception: believes any number is truthy because it is a real value

options.text: the empty string with no characters in it
options.misconception: believes a string is truthy for its type regardless of length

options.text: the empty list that contains no elements
options.misconception: believes a container is truthy for its type regardless of contents

questions.explanation: Strings rate by length, so the empty string is false and a string holding even one character is true, and the character zero counts as a character like any other. Numbers rate by whether they are zero and containers rate by whether they hold anything, so the bare zero and the empty list are both false. The misconception behind the wrong answers is that a value's type settles the question, when it is the value inside the type that counts, which is also why a digit inside a string never becomes a number on its own.
questions.hint: For strings and containers ask whether anything is inside; for numbers ask whether it is zero.

False False False False
options.misconception: believes a string of the digit zero rates the same as the bare integer zero

options.text: True False True True
options.misconception: believes every number and every non-empty container rates as true

options.text: False True False True
options.misconception: believes an empty string still rates as true because it holds a type

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace an or expression and count how many operands are evaluated
questions.stem:
The left operand is a call returning a truthy value, and a counter records only the right call. What does this program print?

right_calls = []
def first():
    return 7
def second():
    right_calls.append(1)
    return 5
result = first() or second()
print(result, len(right_calls))

options.misconception: believes or evaluates both operands and keeps the truthy left value
believes the right value is used even though its call never ran
believes or only returns the left value when the left value is falsy

questions.explanation: The left operand is already truthy, so it can serve as the whole answer and the interpreter never reaches the right operand, which is why the counter stays at zero. The tempting answer that counts one call assumes both operands always run, and the answer that returns the right value is worse, because it reports a value from a call that never happened.
questions.hint: Ask whether the left operand is already good enough to be the answer.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace an and expression and count how many operands are evaluated
questions.stem:
The same two calls are chained with the other operator instead. What does this program print?

right_calls = []
def first():
    return 7
def second():
    right_calls.append(1)
    return 5
result = first() and second()
print(result, len(right_calls))

options.misconception: believes a truthy left operand wins and the right value is discarded
believes a truthy left operand lets and stop before the right call
believes and stops at the first truthy operand like or does

questions.explanation: A truthy left operand cannot stand alone as the answer for this operator, so the right operand is evaluated and its value becomes the result, while the counter shows that the right call did run. The tempting answers mirror or, which short-circuits on exactly the opposite condition: and stops when the left is falsy, because a falsy left already settles the answer.
questions.hint: Ask whether the left operand could serve as the whole answer by itself.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: explain the benefit of chaining a guard with the and operator
questions.stem: A guard is chained in front of a lookup with the and operator, so the lookup only runs when the guard succeeded. What practical benefit is being bought?

options.text: the lookup is skipped when the guard is falsy, so the guard protects it
the lookup always runs first, so the guard is confirmed after the work
options.misconception: believes the left operand of and is the work and the right one is the check

options.text: both sides always run, and the left result is then discarded
options.misconception: believes and evaluates both sides and prefers the right value every time

options.text: both sides must return one object, and the two are compared
options.misconception: believes and is an identity test that requires matching return values

questions.explanation: The operator stops as soon as the left operand rates as false, and a false left side is the signal that the right side has nothing useful to offer, so the right side is never reached. That is what turns a check and a risky operation into one expression in which the risky operation cannot run in the wrong state. The tempting answers either reverse the operand order or assume both sides always run, and both destroy the property the pattern exists to provide.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the right operand when the left one turns out falsy.

questions.learningObjective: trace a single-line conditional that picks between two named values
questions.stem:
One name is assigned by a single-line conditional over a tested remainder. What does this program print?

n = 7
label = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"
print(label)

options.text: the word odd
the word even
options.misconception: believes the value written after the if is what the conditional supplies

options.text: the word True

questions.learningObjective: pair the observed value of a one-line conditional with the mechanism behind it
questions.stem:
The remainder tested here is one, so the condition holds. Which pair names what this program prints and why?

n = 7
print("even" if n % 2 else "odd")

options.text: It prints even, because a nonzero remainder is truthy so the first value is skipped
It prints odd, because a nonzero remainder is truthy so the first value is chosen
options.misconception: confuses which of the two values sits on the true side of the conditional

options.text: It prints even, because a zero remainder is falsy so the first value is chosen
options.misconception: reads the test as holding when the remainder is nonzero and pairs it with the wrong side

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: compute a running total over a range that advances with a step
questions.stem:
A loop walks a range that starts above the stop value and advances by two, adding the square of each value. What is the final value of total?

total = 0
for k in range(2, 10, 2):
    total += k * k
print(total)
questions.explanation: The range supplies two, four, six, and eight, and their squares are four, sixteen, thirty-six, and sixty-four, which sum to one hundred and twenty. The tempting computation squares the stop value as well, or forgets that the stop value itself is never produced, and both errors move the total by a square that the loop never visited.
questions.hint: List the four values the range actually produces before squaring anything.

questions.learningObjective: identify which values a range with a step actually produces
questions.stem: A loop runs its body once for each value in range(1, 10, 2). Which values does the loop variable actually take?

options.misconception: believes the stop value is produced when the step would overshoot it
believes the start value is excluded rather than included
believes the step is ignored because it is a third argument

questions.explanation: A range includes its start and keeps adding the step while the value stays below the stop, so the step of two yields the odd values up to nine, and the stop value itself is never produced. The tempting answer that includes ten comes from thinking a range is inclusive at both ends like some other language's counting forms, and the answer that includes two comes from treating the start as exclusive, which would make it impossible to ask for a range of one value from that number.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace a while loop whose measure drops below its guard before the test fails
questions.stem:
The measure falls by two each pass and the guard only asks whether it is still above zero. What does this program print?

fuel = 7
steps = 0
while fuel > 0:
    fuel -= 2
    steps += 1
print(fuel, steps)

options.misconception: believes the loop stops exactly at zero instead of overshooting it
believes the last pass is skipped once the measure nears the guard
counts the passes that leave the measure positive rather than all of them

questions.explanation: The guard is checked before each pass, and the measure goes seven, five, three, one, then minus one, so the fourth pass still began with a positive value and ran, and only then did the test fail. The tempting answer stops the measure at zero, which would require the step to land there exactly, and a step that does not divide the starting value will always overshoot, so any program relying on a clean landing must test the arithmetic rather than assume it.

questions.learningObjective: trace a loop that stops early on a condition and total only what it visited
questions.stem:
The loop abandons itself as soon as a value's square passes a bound. What does this program print?

total = 0
for k in range(1, 10):
    if k * k > 20:
        break
    total += k
print(total)

options.misconception: believes the break still lets the remaining values be added
adds the breaking value as well before the loop abandons itself
believes the loop counts qualifying values rather than adding them

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: select the statement that ends one pass without ending the loop
questions.stem: A loop body must skip one particular kind of value but keep going over the rest. Which statement does exactly that?

options.text: continue, which ends the current pass and starts the next one
break, which ends the current pass and starts the next one
options.misconception: believes abandoning the loop resumes at the following value

options.text: pass, which ends the current pass and starts the next one
options.misconception: believes the placeholder statement advances the loop on its own

options.text: return, which ends the current pass and starts the next one
options.misconception: believes returning from a loop body hands control to the next value

questions.explanation: Continue abandons the rest of the current pass and hands control straight to the next value, which is exactly the skip-one-kind-of-value behaviour. Break abandons the loop entirely, so the remaining values are never visited, and pass does nothing at all, so the rest of the body still runs. The tempting answers all describe stopping rather than skipping, and a student who reaches for break in a filtering loop silently truncates their data.
questions.hint: One of these statements ends the loop and one does nothing; find the third option.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: explain why a second traversal of a generator expression yields nothing
questions.stem: A generator expression is bound to a name, then traversed twice in a row by a summing call. Explain why the second traversal contributes nothing, and what a program must do instead if it needs the values again.

answer.exemplar: A generator expression does not store its values; it keeps the rule and a record of how far it has already gone. Each pass pulls the next value from that rule and then discards it, and the position only moves forward. Once the first sum has drained the generator, the position is past the end, so the second sum receives nothing and adds zero. A program that needs the values twice must materialise them first, by wrapping the expression in brackets to build a list, so that the second pass walks stored values rather than an exhausted source. That is the trade: a list costs memory up front and can be traversed any number of times, while a generator produces values one at a time and can be traversed only once.

questions.explanation: A generator expression is a producer rather than a container, so it holds a rule and a position rather than the values themselves, and each traversal advances that position and discards what it yields. Draining it therefore leaves nothing behind for a second traversal, and the correct response is to materialise the values into a list when more than one pass is needed. The tempting belief is that an expression is re-evaluated per traversal, but re-evaluation is precisely the behaviour a list gives for free and a generator deliberately does not, since producing values lazily is the whole reason to choose it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the generator stores its values or only remembers how to make them.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: explain when the expression in a parameter list is evaluated
questions.stem: A function declaration gives one parameter a default written as an expression that builds a list. Explain when that expression runs, and why that timing decides whether two calls share one list.

answer.exemplar: The parameter list of a function is part of the declaration, and it is evaluated once, at the moment the declaration itself is executed. The list literal is therefore built a single time, and the object it produces is bound as the default for that parameter. Every later call that omits the argument receives that same object, not a new one, which is why two successive calls that both append to the default find each other's entries already there. The fix is to make the default a value that cannot be mutated, such as the absent marker, and to build the real list inside the body, so the construction genuinely happens per call and no state survives between calls.

questions.explanation: Defaults belong to the declaration rather than to any call, so the expression that produces one is evaluated a single time when the declaration runs and the resulting object is what every later call receives. That is why a mutable default is shared and a shared list accumulates, and the repair is to default to something immutable and construct the real object inside the body. The tempting belief is that the default is a template reapplied per call, but a template would be evaluated per call, and that is exactly the change the fix makes deliberately.
questions.hint: Ask whether the parameter list runs once at the declaration or on every call.

questions.stem:
A student writes two lists with identical contents and claims the program proves they are one shared object. What does this program actually print?

first = [1, 2]
second = [1, 2]
print(first == second, first is second)

options.text: True False
True True
options.misconception: believes matching contents force the interpreter to reuse one object

options.text: False False
options.misconception: believes two separately written lists can never compare equal

options.text: False True
options.misconception: believes the second list is the same object and the values somehow differ

questions.explanation: The two lists were built by separate statements, so they occupy separate storage and the identity test fails, while their contents match exactly so the equality test succeeds. The tempting answer that reports identity as well assumes the interpreter hunts for an existing object whenever a list is constructed, which would make the identity operator useless for the run-time values a program most needs to distinguish, such as two independently fetched results that happen to agree.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two lists were built by one statement or by two.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: analyze a loop whose skip statement a student believes changes nothing
questions.practice: error analysis on a loop skip
questions.stem:
A student believes the skip statement in this loop has no effect and predicts a different total. What does the program actually print?

count = 0
for k in range(5):
    if k < 2:
        count += 1
        continue
    count += 10
print(count)

options.misconception: believes the skip does nothing so both additions run on every pass
counts the two small values as if they contributed the larger amount too
believes the skip also abandons the loop for the remaining passes

questions.explanation: For the two values below two the loop adds one and then abandons the rest of the body, so the larger addition never happens on those passes, and the three remaining values each add ten, giving thirty-two. The tempting answer that treats the skip as a no-op lets both additions run on the two small passes as well, which is exactly the belief the statement exists to correct, and a loop body that does not need the skip is usually better without one.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two additions is reached on a pass that issues the skip.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: analyze a loop body that assigns to its own loop variable and predict the list afterwards
questions.practice: error analysis on a loop variable
questions.stem:
A student multiplies the loop variable inside the body and expects the list itself to be updated. What does this program actually print?

values = [1, 2, 3]
for v in values:
    v = v * 10
print(values)

options.misconception: believes assigning to the loop variable writes through to the list slot
believes the change outlives the pass in which it was made
believes the assignment grows the list by one element

questions.explanation: The loop variable is rebound to a new value on each pass, and rebinding a name is not the same as storing into the list, so the list is left exactly as it was. The tempting answer that shows the scaled values confuses the name with the slot it was read from, and the way to change a list in place is to assign to an indexed position, because that form names the container directly rather than only the name holding the current value.
questions.hint: Ask whether the assignment names a position in the list or only the name holding the value.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: analyze a loop guard written to include the boundary value
questions.practice: error analysis on a loop guard
questions.stem:
A student changes a loop guard to include the boundary and expects the loop to stop once the measure reaches zero. What does this program actually print?

remaining = 3
turns = 0
while remaining >= 0:
    remaining -= 1
    turns += 1
print(remaining, turns)

options.misconception: believes including the boundary still stops the pass that reaches zero
counts the passes that end with a positive measure rather than all of them
believes four passes from three land on zero rather than one below it

questions.explanation: The guard is checked before each pass, so the measure goes three, two, one, zero, and a measure of zero still satisfies the inclusive test, so one more pass runs and drives it to minus one, giving four turns. The tempting answer that stops at zero describes the exclusive form of the guard, and this off-by-one is invisible for any measure that never lands exactly on the boundary, which is why the bug survives in loops whose step does not divide the starting value.
questions.hint: Check the guard before the pass runs, and ask whether zero still satisfies it.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Subscript Used For An Optional Key
questions.learningObjective: analyze a lookup that stops the program when a key is genuinely absent

options.text: It prints KeyError, because the subscript form has no fallback
It prints zero, because the subscript form supplies a default value
options.misconception: believes the subscript quietly falls back to the type's zero value

options.text: It prints None, because the subscript reports an absent key quietly
options.misconception: believes the subscript returns the absent marker rather than raising

options.text: It prints 2, because the subscript falls back to a stored value
options.misconception: believes a miss reuses whatever value happens to be in the dictionary

questions.explanation: The subscript form has no fallback to supply, so a key that was never stored raises a key fault and the handler prints the fault's name. The tempting answers describe the method form, which does take a fallback, and the rewrite looks harmless precisely because it reads as a tidier spelling of the same call; what it actually changes is that a key absent today stops the program rather than producing a value the program can go on with.
questions.hint: Ask whether the form used can produce a value for a key that was never stored.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: pair the span a slice returns with the rule that fixes its length
questions.stem:
A slice is taken from a five-value list and its contents and length are printed. Which pair names both results and the rule behind them?

seq = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(seq[1:4], len(seq[1:4]))

options.text: It prints three values, because the stop position is left out of the span
It prints four values, because the stop position is taken as part of the span
options.misconception: counts the stop position as one of the returned values

options.text: It prints three values, because the start position is left out of the span
options.misconception: treats the start position as excluded rather than the stop position

options.text: It prints four values, because a slice counts positions rather than values
options.misconception: believes the two numbers name the number of values rather than their span

questions.explanation: The span runs from position one up to position four with the stop left out, so it holds the second, third, and fourth values and its length is the difference between the two numbers. The tempting answer that includes the stop position is the most widespread slice bug, and it usually shows up not as a wrong count but as a duplicated boundary element, which is also why clearing a span this way leaves the final value still in place.
questions.hint: Subtract the two bounds to get the length, and the second value is the first one returned.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why A Mutable Default Is Shared
questions.learningObjective: explain why successive calls accumulate into one default object and how to stop it
questions.stem: A function declares a parameter whose default is an empty list, and its body appends to that parameter. Explain why a second call sees the first call's entry, and describe the change that removes the sharing.

answer.exemplar: The parameter list belongs to the declaration, so the list literal is evaluated once when the declaration is executed and the resulting object is bound as the default. A call that omits the argument receives that same object, and the body then appends into it in place, so the mutation outlives the call. The second call omits the argument again, receives the same object, now holding one entry, and appends a second. The repair is to give the parameter a default that cannot be mutated, such as the absent marker, and to build a fresh list inside the body whenever the argument is that marker. The construction then happens per call, so no state survives between calls, and a caller who does pass a list still gets that list appended to exactly as before.

questions.explanation: A default is evaluated once at the declaration, so every call that omits the argument is handed the identical object, and the in-place append makes that sharing observable as a growing result. The repair moves the construction into the body behind a default that cannot be mutated, which turns one shared object into one fresh object per call. The tempting belief is that each call re-evaluates the default, and a program written under that belief will pass its own tests and then fail as soon as a second call arrives.
questions.hint: Decide whether the list literal in the declaration runs once or once per call.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why A Loop Carries An Else
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose of a loop's attached else block and the condition it reports
questions.stem: A for loop searches a list and carries an else block attached to it. Explain what that block is for, and why it can only run when no break was executed.

answer.exemplar: The attached else belongs to the loop as a whole rather than to any single pass, and it runs on normal completion, meaning the loop reached the end of the sequence without leaving early. That makes it the natural home for the one answer the loop's own body never produces: the search finished and found nothing. When the body does find something it issues a break, which abandons the loop and routes around the else block, so the block stays silent precisely when the body has already answered the question. The same shape works for a while loop, where the block reports that the guard failed on its own rather than the body breaking out.

questions.explanation: The attached else runs only on normal completion, so it reports the case the loop's body never handles, namely that the sequence was exhausted without a match. A break abandons the loop and skips the block, which is what keeps the two outcomes from both writing an answer. The tempting reading treats the block as an ordinary statement that happens to sit after the loop, and under that reading it should run in both cases, which would make it useless for reporting the one case a search loop exists to distinguish.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two ways a loop can end the block is attached to.
